pr.title: Bind the last values written into SQL, and remove the escaping
pr.body:
## Summary

This is the follow-up from #19. It binds the last three values that were still written into the SQL text, then removes the escaping helpers. **After this PR, nothing in the server builds SQL from a value.**

## The three queries

| Query | Value | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| `PersistentSecurityRange::Exists` | The name of an auto-ban range: `"Auto-ban: " + user name` from failed logons | The client chooses the value. The escaping held, but it belongs in a parameter. |
| `PersistentIMAPFolder::GetExistsFolderContainingCharacter` | A new IMAP hierarchy delimiter, in `LIKE '%<char>%'` | **A bug on MySQL** (below) |
| `PersistentRuleAction::GetExistsFolderReferenceContainingCharacter` | The same, for rule actions' folders | Same bug |

**The MySQL bug:** a backslash was escaped to `'%\\%'`. MySQL then read the pattern's backslash as LIKE's default escape character, so a folder whose name contained `\` was never found. The delimiter could therefore be changed to `\` even though a folder already used it.

All three now bind their values. The LIKE checks bind a pattern made by the new `SQLStatement::EscapeLike`, with an explicit `ESCAPE '/'`. That is the form the greylisting query already uses, and every database reads it the same way.

## Removed

- `SQLStatement::Escape`, and `EscapeString` on `DALConnection` and its four implementations. Nothing called `EscapeString`.
- The escaping of raw columns (`NULL`, `current_timestamp`). These are SQL the server writes itself, now appended as they are rather than run through value escaping.

## Also

- `Property::WriteStringSetting_` wrote the setting's name into the SQL with `Formatter::Format("settingname = '{0}'")` and no escaping. The name is always one of the server's own, but it's now bound like the value, as the integer and boolean writes next to it already do.
- Many queries still build a `WHERE` clause with `Format("xid = %I64d", id)` (integer IDs), or append SQL the server writes itself (timestamps, IP comparisons). None of them can be injected, because no text value goes into them. Converting them to parameters is a Phase 5 cleanup, not a security fix.

## Tests

- `IMAP.HierarchyDelimiter.TestDelimiterChangeIsRefusedWhenAFolderContainsIt`: with a folder named `Back\slash`, changing the delimiter to `\` is refused, while a change to `/` goes through.
- `IMAP.HierarchyDelimiter.TestDelimiterChangeIsRefusedWhenARuleFolderContainsIt`: the same for a rule action's folder.
- `Security.AutoBan.TestIPRangeNameWithQuoteInUserName`: a user named `o'brien@example.test` is banned while a range with that name already exists. The new range must be named `... (1)`, which works only if `Exists` finds the name with the quote in it.
- `SQLStatementTester`: `EscapeLike`.

On the old code, the two delimiter tests are expected to fail on MySQL, for the reason above, and pass on the other databases.

commit.message:
Bind the last values written into SQL, and remove the escaping

Three queries still wrote a value into the SQL through SQLStatement::Escape:

- PersistentSecurityRange::Exists, with the name of an auto-ban range, which
  carries the user name of the failed logons - a value the client chooses.
- PersistentIMAPFolder::GetExistsFolderContainingCharacter and
  PersistentRuleAction::GetExistsFolderReferenceContainingCharacter, which
  check that no folder contains a new IMAP hierarchy delimiter, with
  LIKE '%<character>%'. On MySQL that did not work for a backslash: escaped
  as '%\\%', MySQL read the pattern's backslash as its LIKE escape, so a folder
  whose name contained one was never found, and the delimiter could be changed
  to a character in use.

They bind their values now. The two LIKE checks bind a pattern made with the
new SQLStatement::EscapeLike and name ESCAPE '/', as the greylisting query
already does, which every database reads the same way.

With that, nothing writes a value into the SQL, so SQLStatement::Escape and the
EscapeString of DALConnection and the four connections, which nothing called,
are removed. SQLStatement's raw columns - NULL and current_timestamp, SQL the
server itself writes - are appended as they are, rather than passed through an
escaping meant for values.

Tests:
- HierarchyDelimiter: the delimiter cannot become a backslash that a folder
  name, or the folder of a rule action, contains, while a change to a character
  in no folder goes through.
- AutoBan: the range of a user named o'brien@example.test, with a range of that
  name already there, takes the name "... (1)".
- SQLStatementTester: EscapeLike.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Bind the setting name in Property::WriteStringSetting_

The update wrote the setting's name into the SQL with Formatter::Format and no
escaping. The name is always one of the server's own, but nothing should be
written into the SQL unescaped, and the integer and boolean writes beside it
already bind it.

issue.title: Protect secrets with AES-256-GCM under a per-installation DPAPI key (1.2a)

repository.name: ArzoieMail
repository.description: ArzoieMail is a free, open-source email server for Windows, forked from hMailServer. It supports SMTP, IMAP and POP3, plus anti-spam, anti-virus, DKIM, SSL/TLS, backups, scripting and a COM API. Named after my daughter Arzoie and maintained in Delhi, India.

license.name: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0

issue.body:
## Summary

Phase 1.2a: the secrets the server has to read back are now encrypted with **AES-256-GCM under a key generated for each installation**, protected by Windows DPAPI. Until now they were Blowfish-encrypted with `THIS_KEY_IS_NOT_SECRET`, a key in the source code, so anyone with a copy of `hMailServer.ini`, the database or a backup could decrypt them.

Secrets covered:
- the database password in `hMailServer.ini`;
- the SMTP relay password and the SRS secret (`hm_settings`);
- the passwords of external (fetch) accounts (`hm_fetchaccounts`);
- route authentication passwords (`hm_routes`).

## Design

| | |
|---|---|
| **Cipher** | AES-256-GCM (OpenSSL): a random 12-byte nonce per value and a 16-byte tag; the prefix and key ID are authenticated as associated data |
| **Key** | 32 random bytes per installation, stored in `hMailServer.ini` as `[Security] SecretKey`, DPAPI-protected with machine scope. Only this computer can unprotect it; the service account and the administrator both can. |
| **Stored format** | `aes1:<key id>:<base64(nonce ‖ ciphertext ‖ tag)>`. The key ID is the first 8 hex digits of SHA-256(key). |
| **Old values** | A Blowfish value (hex digits only) is still read, so nothing breaks before the migration has run |
| **Migration** | `SecretMigration` runs at every start, after the database connects and before the configuration loads. It re-protects every Blowfish secret in `hMailServer.ini` and the three tables, and each update is guarded by the old value. After the first start it only reads. |
| **ini type** | The database password is written with `PasswordEncryption=5` (`Crypt::ETSecret`) |

`Crypt::ETSecret` routes through the new `SecretProtector`. `ETBlowFish` stays only where Blowfish is still needed: the COM `BlowfishEncrypt`/`BlowfishDecrypt` methods, and account passwords that very old versions stored that way.

## Failure handling

All of these are reported once each, as error 5739:

- **The key can't be created, or `hMailServer.ini` can't be written** (for example an old installation under Program Files): secrets stay Blowfish-encrypted. They are never encrypted under a key that would be lost at the next start.
- **The stored key can't be unprotected** (an ini file copied from another computer): the key is never replaced. New secrets stay Blowfish-encrypted until the key from the original computer is imported (1.2b).
- **A value protected under another installation's key** (two servers sharing a database): it is recognised by its key ID and refused with a clear message, not decrypted into garbage.

## Not in this PR (next)

- **1.2b:** export and import of the key under a passphrase, through the COM API and the Administrator. It's needed when moving a server, restoring `hMailServer.ini` on another machine, or giving servers that share a database the same key.
- **1.2c:** backups protected by a passphrase. Today a backup keeps fetch-account and route passwords encrypted under the installation's key, and stores the relay password and SRS secret **in plain text**, which is existing behaviour.

## Tests

- `SecretProtectorTester` (class test):
  - round trips of empty, ASCII and non-ASCII values;
  - two protections of the same value differ (fresh nonce);
  - a changed value is refused, and so is a value under another key;
  - Blowfish values are still read, and plain text is not mistaken for a secret.
- `SecretMigrationTester` (class test): every secret in the database and in `hMailServer.ini` is protected under the installation's key.
- `API.Secrets.TestBlowfishRoutePasswordIsMigratedAndStillWorks`:
  - stores a route password Blowfish-encrypted, as an earlier version would have;
  - calls `Reinitialize()`, so the migration runs;
  - runs the class tests, which check it was migrated;
  - delivers through the route and asserts that the simulated SMTP server received the original password.
- `API.Secrets.TestProtectedRoutePasswordAuthenticates`: a password set through the API is the one sent on AUTH.
- `SmtpServerSimulator` gains `AuthPassword`, the decoded AUTH LOGIN password.

## CI follow-ups in this PR

- **ini values over 255 characters:** `IniFileSettings::ReadIniSettingString_` read every value through a 255-character buffer. The DPAPI-protected key is longer, so it came back truncated, the read-back check failed, and every installation fell back to Blowfish. The buffer now grows until the value fits.
- **ASCII route passwords in the tests:** the route tests failed on non-ASCII passwords because the SMTP client sends AUTH LOGIN credentials in the system code page rather than UTF-8 (`ä` arrives as one non-UTF-8 byte, `✓` is dropped). That's an existing SMTP-client bug, not related to how the secret is stored, and it's now a follow-up. `SecretProtectorTester` covers non-ASCII secrets.

**Result:** green on all three databases, with 1,298 tests: 1,189 passed, 0 failed.

## Merge note

`Property.cpp` is also changed by #20, so whichever is merged second needs a small rebase.
